q: On which date was the decimal coinage system introduced in India?
explain: Decimal coinage, with the rupee divided into 100 paise, began on 1 April 1957 under the Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955.

q: The highest denomination note ever printed by the RBI was the ₹10,000 note. It was first printed in which year?
explain: The ₹10,000 note was first printed in 1938 and again in 1954. It was demonetised in 1946 and again in 1978.

q: Which of the following is the highest-valued currency in comparison to the Indian rupee?
explain: The Kuwaiti dinar (KWD) is widely called the world's strongest currency; one dinar was worth roughly ₹267 at the time of writing, more than the pound or dollar.

q: The Indian currency system was converted to a decimal system by which law, in force from 1 April 1957?
explain: The Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955 brought in decimal coinage, effective 1 April 1957. The Acts of 1946 and 1949 deal with banking.

q: The ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes that lost legal tender status on 8 November 2016 belonged to which series?
explain: Government Notification no. 2652 withdrew the legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series issued up to 8 November 2016.

q: All Indian currency notes bear the Governor of the RBI's signature except which one?
explain: The ₹1 note is issued by the Government of India and carries the signature of the Finance Secretary, not the RBI Governor.

q: Distribution and administration of currency in India is done by which institution as an agent of the Government of India?
explain: The RBI manages currency under the RBI Act, 1934, acting as the agent of the Government for issue and distribution.

q: In which year was paper currency introduced in India by the British government?
explain: Paper currency was introduced in 1861 through the Paper Currency Act. The RBI itself came much later, in 1935.

q: Which term refers to withdrawing a currency from circulation to curb black money and unaccounted cash?
explain: Demonetisation means stripping a currency note of legal tender status. Devaluation is a fall in a currency's official exchange value.

q: In which year, before 2016, were high-value currency notes demonetised in India?
explain: High-value notes of ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 were demonetised in 1978. An earlier demonetisation took place in 1946.

q: Up to what denomination can coins be issued under the Coinage Act, 2011?
explain: Coins can be issued up to ₹1,000, while notes can go up to ₹10,000 under the RBI Act.

q: The ₹2000 banknote of 2016 carries the image of which of the following on its reverse?
explain: The reverse of the ₹2000 note shows Mangalyaan, the Mars Orbiter Mission. The Red Fort appears on the ₹500 note.

q: In which Karnataka city is an RBI banknote press located?
explain: The RBI's subsidiary BRBNMPL runs presses at Mysuru (Karnataka) and Salboni (West Bengal).

q: From which law does the Reserve Bank of India derive its role in currency management?
explain: The RBI Act, 1934 gives the RBI its role in managing banknotes. The Coinage Act, 2011 deals with coins, which are the Government's responsibility.

q: Who is responsible for the designing and minting of coins in India?
explain: Coinage vests with the Government of India under the Coinage Act, 2011. The RBI only handles distribution of coins.

q: Under Section 25 of the RBI Act, 1934, who approves the design of banknotes?
options: The Central Government on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board
explain: The design must be approved by the Central Government on the recommendation of the Central Board of the RBI.

q: The RBI's liability to pay the value of a banknote, shown by the 'I promise to pay' clause, arises from what?
options: A contract between holder and the RBI
Statutory provisions, Section 26 of the RBI Act
explain: Section 26 of the RBI Act makes the Bank liable to pay the value of the note on demand. The obligation is statutory, not contractual.

q: What is the highest denomination of banknote that the RBI Act, 1934 permits?
explain: Notes of ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 or other denominations notified by the Centre are allowed, but none above ₹10,000.

q: Besides Hindi at the centre and English on the reverse, how many languages appear in the language panel of an Indian banknote?
explain: Fifteen languages appear in the panel, in addition to Hindi and English.

q: From which date were 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 25 paise coins withdrawn from circulation and ceased to be legal tender?
explain: These small coins were withdrawn with effect from 30 June 2011.

q: Why was the printing of ₹2 and ₹5 banknotes discontinued?
options: These denominations are now issued as coins
Parliament abolished them by an Act
explain: Because ₹2 and ₹5 are now available as coins, there was no need to print notes of those values.

q: Government Notification no. 2652 of 8 November 2016 withdrew the legal tender status of which banknotes?
explain: The notification withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series. The new ₹2000 note was introduced afterwards.

q: Indian banknote paper is made from which material?
explain: Currency paper in India is composed of cotton and cotton rag.

q: Which of the following describes a soiled banknote?
options: A note that is dirty and slightly cut
A note with a missing portion
A note that has been washed or altered
A note that has been burnt
explain: Soiled notes are dirty and slightly cut. Missing portions make a note mutilated, washing or alteration makes it imperfect, and burnt notes need special handling at an Issue Office.

q: A banknote that has a missing portion or consists of more than two pieces is called
explain: A mutilated note has a missing portion or is in more than two pieces; its refund value is paid under the RBI (Note Refund) Rules.

q: Where can excessively soiled, brittle or burnt notes be exchanged?
options: At any public sector bank branch
At any private sector bank branch
Only at an RBI Issue Office
explain: Such notes are exchanged only at an RBI Issue Office, through the Claims Section of the Issue Department.

q: To exchange a soiled note at the counter of a public sector bank branch, what is the requirement?
options: A prescribed form with an affidavit
No form needs to be filled
A fee of 10% of the note value
explain: Soiled and mutilated notes can be exchanged at counters of public sector banks, currency chest branches of private banks and RBI Issue Offices without filling any form.

q: In the context of exchanging mutilated notes, what does TLR stand for?
explain: A Triple Lock Receptacle is a box at the RBI where the public can deposit mutilated notes in a TLR cover against a paper token.

q: A note of ₹10 or more in two pieces, with the number on both pieces, is treated as
explain: Two pieces with the numbers on both ends make the note soiled. More than two pieces, or a missing portion, makes it mutilated.

q: Which of the following is an imperfect banknote?
options: A note with a missing corner
A note that is wholly or partly obliterated, shrunk, washed or altered
A note of a withdrawn series
A note with a different language panel
explain: Imperfect notes are obliterated, shrunk, washed, altered or indecipherable; the definition excludes mutilated notes.

q: The banknote presses at Nashik and Dewas are owned by which organisation?
options: Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India
explain: SPMCIL owns the Nashik and Dewas presses, while the RBI's subsidiary BRBNMPL owns those at Mysuru and Salboni.

q: In which state is the RBI-owned note press at Salboni located?
explain: Salboni is in West Bengal. Nashik is in Maharashtra, Dewas in Madhya Pradesh and Mysuru in Karnataka.

q: Which of the following cities does NOT have a government mint producing coins?
explain: Coins are minted at Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Noida. Nagpur has an RBI issue office but no mint.

q: Which of the following RBI offices initially receives coins from the mints?
explain: The mint-linked offices are Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai and New Delhi; they pass coins on to other RBI offices.

q: Which sequence shows the correct flow of currency to the public?
options: Mints → bank branches → currency chests → public
Bank branches → RBI offices → printing presses → public
Printing presses → RBI offices → currency chests → bank branches → public
Currency chests → printing presses → RBI offices → public
explain: Notes come from presses to RBI offices, then to currency chests, then to bank branches and finally the public.

q: Where are small coins stocked before reaching bank branches?
explain: Notes and rupee coins are stocked at currency chests, while small coins are stored at small coin depots.

q: Who is responsible for moving currency from a currency chest to a bank branch?
explain: RBI officials accompany remittances to chests, but movement from chest to branch is done by the bank concerned.

q: Which of the following goes against the RBI's Clean Note Policy?
options: Keeping notes flat in a wallet
Handing over notes without any marks
explain: The public is asked not to staple notes, not to write on or stamp them, and to store them safely.

q: Which was an objective of the demonetisation of high-value notes?
options: Stopping the funding of terrorism through counterfeit notes and fighting corruption
explain: The two stated aims were to stop the funding of militancy and terrorism (counterfeit notes) and to fight corruption.

q: ₹10,000 notes were demonetised in 1946 and again in which year?
explain: The ₹10,000 note was printed in 1938 and 1954 and demonetised in 1946 and then in 1978.

q: In 1949 the Banking Companies Act was amended and renamed as which Act?
explain: The Banking Companies Act, 1949 was amended and renamed the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

q: When a member of the public drops mutilated notes in a Triple Lock Receptacle, what do they get at the time?
explain: The notes are put in a TLR cover with particulars filled in and deposited against a paper token.

q: One Indian rupee consists of how many paise?
explain: One rupee equals 100 paise.

q: What feature of the rupee symbol ₹ is correct?
options: A single horizontal line below the letter
A double horizontal line at the top, resembling the Devanagari 'Ra' and Latin 'R'
A circle around the letter R
explain: The symbol blends the Devanagari letter Ra and the Latin capital R, with a double horizontal line at the top.
